documents.title: Rice Blast Disease: Symptoms and Identification
documents.content: Rice blast is a fungal disease that can affect rice at several growth stages, from seedlings to tillering and panicle heading. On leaves, early symptoms may appear as small bluish-green flecks that develop into spindle-shaped lesions with grey centres and dark-brown margins, particularly under moist conditions. As lesions grow and merge, leaves may dry and wither. Lesions can also occur on leaf sheaths and nodes. Node infections may girdle the stem, cause breakage, and lead to death of plant parts above the affected node. Infection near the base of the plant or panicle neck may cause white or poorly developed panicles. Neck lesions are often greyish-brown and may cause the panicle to fall over. Infection timing can affect grain formation and quality. Lesion appearance and size can vary among rice varieties.

documents.title: Rice Bacterial Leaf Blight: Symptoms and Identification
documents.content: Rice bacterial leaf blight is caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae. In mature plants, early symptoms may include water-soaked, translucent lesions near leaf margins. Lesions can lengthen and widen, develop wavy margins, and turn straw yellow. Advanced infection can cause large areas of the leaf blade to become white or straw-coloured. Seedlings may show yellow marginal spots, and a severe seedling phase can cause wilting. Some young lesions may produce milky or opaque bacterial droplets in the early morning.

documents.title: Rice Brown Spot: Symptoms and Identification
documents.content: Rice brown spot is a fungal disease associated with Bipolaris oryzae, historically also referred to as Helminthosporium oryzae. Symptoms can include round, oval, or irregular brown spots on leaves. Spots may merge and cause affected tissue to wither. Brown or greyish-brown discolouration may also occur near the neck, and grains may develop reddish-brown discolouration.

documents.title: Rice Sheath Blight: Symptoms and Identification
documents.content: Rice sheath blight is a fungal disease caused by Rhizoctonia solani. It commonly affects rice from tillering to heading. Initial symptoms are often found on leaf sheaths near the water level, where greenish-grey, oval, elliptical, or irregular lesions develop. As lesions enlarge, their centres may become greyish-white with darker brown or purple-brown borders. Lesions may spread to upper parts of the plant and merge, causing leaves to die. Severe infection can affect multiple leaves and tillers and may contribute to poorly filled grains.

documents.title: Cotton Bacterial Blight: Symptoms and Identification
documents.content: Cotton bacterial blight is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. malvacearum. Symptoms can vary with the growth stage. On leaves, small dark-green water-soaked spots may develop, often restricted by veins and veinlets, giving them an angular appearance. Spots may later become reddish-brown. Veins and veinlets may turn black, and affected leaves may become crinkled, twist inward, wither, or fall. Symptoms can also affect seedlings and other plant parts.

documents.title: Cotton Alternaria Leaf Blight: Symptoms and Identification
documents.content: Cotton Alternaria leaf blight is associated with the fungus Alternaria macrospora. Symptoms can include small pale-to-brown, round or irregular spots on leaves. Spots may show a central lesion surrounded by concentric rings. Multiple spots can merge into larger blighted areas, and affected leaves may become brittle and fall. Spots may also occur on bracts and bolls.

documents.content: TNAU describes maize leaf blight associated with Exserohilum turcicum and Helminthosporium maydis. Reported symptoms include long, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions on lower leaves; slender, oblong lesions tapering at the ends; lesions running parallel to leaf margins and sometimes merging; and leaves becoming greyish-green and brittle. TNAU notes that wet, humid, cool weather can favour disease development. The source groups the pathogens under one leaf-blight heading, so symptoms alone should not be treated as definitive pathogen identification.
